title: Effects and Data Loading
summary: An Effect helps a React component stay in step with something outside its normal page drawing.
introduction: An Effect helps a React component stay in step with something outside its normal page drawing. For example, a part might start a timer and stop it when it is no longer needed. Learn both the setup step and the clean-up step.
learningObjectives: Run code after render with useEffect and control when it re-runs with dependencies
Return a cleanup function for timers, listeners and subscriptions
Explain why Strict Mode runs effects twice in development
Load data in an effect without race conditions and recognize cases that need no effect

blocks.text: An effect is a function React calls after it has committed your JSX to the DOM. Because it runs after render, it may do things that would be wrong during render: read or change the DOM, start a timer, subscribe to something, send a request. The classic first example keeps the document title in sync with state.

blocks.title: Title.jsx
Browser tab title after two clicks

blocks.text: The second argument is the **dependency array**. After a render, React re-runs the effect only if one of the listed values changed (compared with `Object.is`). The array must list every prop, state or derived value the effect reads; the `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` lint rule in the Vite template checks this for you.

rows: once, after the first render (and again only if the component remounts)
after the first render and whenever `a` or `b` changes

blocks.text: Anything an effect starts must be stopped when the component unmounts, and also before the effect runs again with new dependencies. Return a function from the effect; React calls it at exactly those moments.

blocks.title: Clock.jsx

blocks.text: The updater form `setSeconds((s) => s + 1)` matters here: the interval callback was created once and would otherwise keep seeing the `seconds` value from the first render. Event listeners (`window.addEventListener`), subscriptions and an `AbortController` for requests follow the same start-in-effect, stop-in-cleanup shape.

blocks.title: Common mistake: no cleanup, or an effect that never settles
blocks.text: An interval without `clearInterval` keeps running after the component is gone, and in Strict Mode you get two of them, so the counter jumps by two every second. The other classic is an effect with no dependency array that calls a state setter: every render runs the effect, the setter causes a render, and the component loops forever. Always ask: what starts here, and what stops it?

In development, `<StrictMode>` mounts every component, runs its effects, immediately runs the cleanups, then runs the effects again. This simulates a component being hidden and shown and exposes effects whose cleanup is missing or wrong. It happens only in development, never in production.

blocks.title: Console in development with Strict Mode

blocks.text: If the double log makes you want to remove Strict Mode, resist: an effect that cannot survive being run twice has a bug that will show up in production the moment the component remounts.

Fetching is the most common effect, and the most common place for a subtle bug: if the dependencies change while a request is in flight, the old response may arrive after the new one and overwrite it. The fix is an `ignore` flag that the cleanup flips.

blocks.text: Three states (loading, error, ready) cover every outcome, and the `ok` check matters because `fetch` only rejects on network failure, not on a 404 or 500. In Strict Mode this component sends the request twice during development; the first response is ignored thanks to the flag. The [data fetching lesson](/tutorials/react/data-fetching) shows how a library removes this boilerplate and adds caching.
You might not need an effect
Effects are for synchronizing with something **outside** React. Two kinds of code often end up in effects by mistake and belong elsewhere:

rows: A value computed from props or state (a total, a filtered list)
Compute it during render, or with `useMemo` if it is expensive
Reacting to a user action (submit, click)
Do the work in the event handler
Resetting state when a prop changes
Give the component a `key` so it remounts, or compute the state from the prop
Notifying the parent of a state change
Call the parent's callback in the same handler that sets the state

blocks.text: A quick test: if you can describe the code as "when X happens, do Y" and X is a user event, write a handler. If it is "keep Z in sync with the outside world", it is an effect.

questions.question: When does an effect with `[]` as its dependency array run in a production build?
questions.explanation: An empty array means no dependency can ever change, so the effect runs once after the first render and its cleanup runs when the component unmounts.
options: Once, after the component first renders

questions.question: `fetch` rejects its promise when the server responds with status 500.
questions.explanation: `fetch` only rejects on network errors. A 500 or 404 resolves normally with `response.ok === false`, which is why the examples check `ok` and throw.

seo.title: React useEffect – Dependencies, Cleanup and Data
seo.description: Learn useEffect in React 19: dependency arrays, cleanup, why Strict Mode runs effects twice, loading data without race conditions and when not to use an effect.
